terms.definition: The independent control that checks whether a specific identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource before a tool executes it.
terms.example: Allow a sandbox test run; deny a request to change production data.

terms.definition: How much eligible work actually uses the AI-assisted process. Tool access or license counts alone do not measure this.
terms.example: Half of eligible test-writing work uses the assistant during the measured period.

terms.definition: A system that uses an AI model to choose steps and call tools toward a task. Its ability to propose an action is separate from permission to execute it.
terms.example: A test author chooses a repository search, then asks to run a test in a sandbox.

terms.definition: The AI-enabled product being evaluated, including its model, prompts, retrieval and tools. It is distinct from the assistant that creates tests.
terms.example: A customer-support agent is the application under test.

terms.definition: Using AI to help people design tests, investigate failures and review security findings. People still need evidence that the resulting work is correct.
terms.example: An assistant drafts a payment test; an engineer checks its expected result.

terms.definition: A defined way for software to request data or actions from another system. In this design, a tool call uses a bounded interface rather than unrestricted system access.
terms.example: A sandbox API accepts a test artifact and returns a run identifier.

terms.definition: Work that identifies, prevents and fixes security weaknesses in software and its delivery process.
terms.example: Triage a scanner finding, verify that the proposed fix blocks the attack, and retain review evidence.

terms.definition: Checking who or what is making a request. Establishing identity does not establish permission for every action.
terms.example: Verify the service identity that submitted a sandbox run request.

terms.definition: Deciding whether an identity is allowed to perform the requested action on the requested resource under the current policy.
terms.example: A known service identity may read test fixtures but may not access production accounts.

terms.definition: The measured starting point used for a comparison, including the work, people, quality and effort counted.
terms.example: Measure current test-writing and review time before introducing the assistant.

terms.definition: A defined task set and measurement method used to compare performance. Results apply to those tasks and conditions before any broader inference is made.
terms.example: Success on a public coding set does not establish savings on the bank’s regression work.

terms.definition: The share of positive released capacity that can become a financial benefit through an agreed spending change in the relevant period.
terms.example: An approved reduction in contractor scope converts part of the released capacity into lower spending.

terms.definition: Evidence supporting the claim that an intervention changed an outcome, using a design that addresses alternative explanations. Its scope still depends on the study.
terms.example: A randomized comparison estimates a tool’s effect for the studied participants and tasks.

terms.definition: Automated steps that integrate code and prepare it for release. CD can mean delivery or deployment; this site’s release path retains an explicit approval decision.
terms.example: A code change triggers tests and evidence collection before an approved release.

terms.definition: A range calculated by a statistical method to express uncertainty in an estimate. A 95% method is designed to cover the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions.
terms.example: A wide interval signals that the data allow a broad range of effect sizes.

terms.definition: The proposed component that supplies relevant, versioned material the task is allowed to access. Retrieved text remains untrusted as instructions.
terms.example: Supply the approved API contract, excluding another team’s restricted customer records.

terms.definition: Preventing an otherwise planned cost, measured against an approved counterfactual spending plan. It differs from reducing current spending.
terms.example: Absorb planned demand without an additional hire that was in the approved workforce plan.

terms.definition: The existing tools that hold requirements, code, builds, tests and change records. They supply versioned inputs to the proposed platform.
terms.example: The repository provides a commit; the ticket system provides its acceptance criteria.

terms.definition: A check that applies fixed rules to the same inputs and conditions, producing a repeatable result. Its usefulness still depends on choosing the right rule.
terms.example: Assert that an invalid payment returns status 422 and writes zero payment records.

terms.definition: A compact value calculated from content to identify a particular version and detect changes. It does not show that the content is safe or correct.
terms.example: A changed test file has a different digest, so its earlier evaluation cannot be reused as proof.

terms.definition: A change in the inputs, environment or behavior that can make earlier evaluation results less representative of current use.
terms.example: Customers begin asking about a new product that the evaluation set does not cover.

terms.definition: Probing a running application for security weaknesses by observing its responses. Scope and authorization matter before running these checks.
terms.example: Send authorized test requests to a sandbox endpoint and inspect its responses.

terms.definition: The share of an activity that fits the agreed AI use case and its control constraints. It is an input to the site’s savings model.
terms.example: Exclude tasks needing restricted data when the pilot cannot access that data.

terms.definition: The written agreement on what is being tested, for whom, which failures matter, how results are scored and what thresholds must be met.
terms.example: Require the payment system to reject negative amounts and create no payment record.

terms.definition: A record of the exact artifacts, configuration, evaluation data and checks used in an evaluation. Changes can invalidate earlier results.
terms.example: Record the model, prompt, dataset, runner and candidate digests for run EVAL-042.

terms.definition: The proposed component that runs an AI application against defined cases and scoring rules, then records its behavior and results.
terms.example: Check answer correctness, permitted tool use and refusal behavior for a support agent.

terms.definition: The proposed store of linked inputs, decisions and results that lets a reviewer reconstruct what happened. Recording an outcome does not by itself make that outcome trustworthy.
terms.example: Link the task, permission decision, artifact version and sandbox result in one reviewable record.

terms.definition: A predefined alternative when an AI step or dependency cannot safely continue. A rollback specifically restores an earlier state; a fallback may route work to a person instead.
terms.example: Stop the agent and send the task to a reviewer when the required context is unavailable.

terms.definition: A result that fails to flag a problem or positive condition that is actually present.
terms.example: A scan reports no issue even though an exploitable flaw exists.

terms.definition: A result that flags a problem or positive condition when that condition is absent. Interpret “positive” according to the task.
terms.example: A security scanner reports a vulnerability that investigation shows is not present.

terms.definition: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without a relevant change to the code under test. Investigate causes before changing assertions or suppressing it.
terms.example: A timing-sensitive test fails intermittently when a shared environment is busy.

terms.definition: Connecting an AI output to the supplied source material so its claims can be checked against that material. Source support alone does not prove the source is correct.
terms.example: A generated test cites the exact requirement version that defines the expected behavior.

terms.definition: A reduction in spending recognized through an agreed Finance process. The site distinguishes this from time saved or capacity redeployed.
terms.example: An approved contract renewal costs less because less work is purchased.

terms.definition: Evaluation cases kept separate from the examples used to develop or tune the system, so the assessment is less influenced by those choices.
terms.example: Reserve unseen payment edge cases for the final pilot evaluation.

terms.definition: An identifier a service uses to recognize repeated requests for the same operation and avoid duplicate effects under its defined contract.
terms.example: After a timeout, check the original run using the same key before attempting a retry.

terms.definition: Comparing a model judge’s scores with expert ratings on representative cases, then checking disagreement, bias and consistency.
terms.example: Inspect cases where the judge passes an answer that experts rate as incorrect.

terms.definition: An AI model that generates or analyzes language and code from its input. A fluent response can still be incorrect.
terms.example: A model writes a test from a requirement but may invent the expected result.

terms.definition: Giving an identity only the access needed for its task, limited by resource, action and time where possible.
terms.example: Permit one test run in an isolated project until the task’s authorization expires.

terms.definition: A language model used to score an output against a rubric. Its scores need checks against expert judgment and known failure cases.
terms.example: A judge scores answer completeness; experts verify whether it overlooks unsupported claims.

terms.definition: Deliberately introducing small faults to check whether tests detect them. Detection adds evidence about test strength; it does not prove all real defects will be caught.
terms.example: Change “reject negative amounts” to “accept negative amounts” and check that the test fails.

terms.definition: Benefits remaining after the relevant AI, platform, evaluation, governance and other costs are deducted. State whether the result values effort or represents cash impact.
terms.example: Subtract pilot costs from captured benefit; value any added effort separately from actual cash spending.

terms.definition: The share of baseline human effort removed after counting AI-assisted work, review, correction and additional controls. It can be negative.
terms.example: A 10-hour task becomes 6 hours of work plus 2 hours of review: net task saving is 20%.

terms.definition: An identity assigned to a service or workload rather than a person, with an owner and managed permissions.
terms.example: The test runner uses its own scoped identity instead of an engineer’s broad credentials.

terms.definition: Evidence from observed behavior or reported experience without assigning the intervention. Differences may reflect other factors as well as AI use.
terms.example: Teams using AI report faster delivery, but may also differ in skills or platform maturity.

terms.definition: One numerical estimate of an outcome or effect. It should be read with the study’s method, uncertainty and measurement unit.
terms.example: An estimated time reduction needs its task definition and uncertainty, not only a percentage.

terms.definition: The share of positive findings that are correct: true positives divided by all reported positives. High precision means fewer false alarms among the findings.
terms.example: Of 10 reported vulnerabilities, 8 are confirmed: precision is 80%.

terms.definition: An attempt to make an AI system follow attacker-supplied instructions, including instructions embedded in retrieved material or tool results.
terms.example: A repository file tells the assistant to ignore its task and disclose a secret.

terms.definition: Testing and monitoring an AI application itself: its answers, use of tools, resistance to attacks and behavior when something fails.
terms.example: Check whether a support agent retrieves an allowed document and refuses an unauthorized action.

terms.definition: The proposed execution environment that coordinates AI-assisted QE work and drafts candidate artifacts within time and cost limits.
terms.example: Draft a test, request a sandbox run, and revise it using the failure evidence.

terms.definition: Activities that build confidence that quality requirements will be met, including agreed processes, reviews and checks. This site uses QE for the broader engineering approach and retains QA where sources or cost models use that label.
terms.example: Review whether a release followed its agreed testing and approval process.

terms.definition: Building quality into delivery through clear requirements, prevention, testing and feedback. On this site, QE includes both conventional software and AI behavior.
terms.example: Define the payment rule before writing code, test it, then monitor failures after release.

terms.definition: The minimum acceptable quality and safety conditions that must hold while testing a productivity improvement. Mandatory gates cannot be offset by time saved.
terms.example: Hold the pilot when a required security check fails, even if tests are produced faster.

terms.definition: The share of actual positive cases detected: true positives divided by all actual positives. Measuring it requires knowing which cases truly contain the condition.
terms.example: A seeded set contains 10 vulnerabilities and the tool finds 8: recall is 80%.

terms.definition: A curated, versioned collection of cases rerun after changes to detect previously addressed failures returning.
terms.example: Add a reviewed negative-payment case after a defect investigation.

terms.definition: The accountable person or process that decides whether the evidence and required approvals support release. In the demo, human approval is independent of generation.
terms.example: Hold the change when a mandatory check fails, even if the generated code looks plausible.

terms.definition: Human time made available after net task savings, eligible work and actual adoption are accounted for. It may be redeployed without reducing spending.
terms.example: A team uses freed hours to reduce its backlog while the payroll stays the same.

terms.definition: Finding relevant material and supplying it to a model as context for its response. Retrieval must respect the requesting identity’s permissions.
terms.example: Retrieve the approved payment specification before drafting its tests.

terms.definition: Execution and validation inside an isolated environment with limited access and resources. Passing these checks provides evidence for review.
terms.example: Run the candidate test against known good behavior and a deliberately faulty implementation.

terms.definition: An explicit set of assumptions used to explore possible outcomes. A scenario is not a measured result or a forecast unless evidence supports that use.
terms.example: Compare lower adoption or higher review effort while keeping the other model inputs fixed.

terms.definition: Analyzing source code or related artifacts for potential security weaknesses without running the application being examined.
terms.example: Flag a potentially unsafe data flow from user input to a database query.

terms.definition: The place where a person submits a scoped task and inspects the result. It records the request and its owner.
terms.example: An engineer asks for tests for one payment endpoint.

terms.definition: Recorded operational measurements and events used to understand system behavior. Logs, timing and tool-use records can support investigation and monitoring.
terms.example: Track failed requests, tool denials, evaluation scores and cost per run.

terms.definition: A measure of which parts of a system or requirement set tests exercise. High coverage does not establish that the assertions detect incorrect behavior.
terms.example: A test reaches the rejection branch but never checks whether a payment was created.

terms.definition: The basis for deciding whether observed behavior is correct. It should come from an independent rule or trusted reference, rather than simply repeat the generated code’s assumptions.
terms.example: The payment specification requires HTTP 422 and no new payment for a negative amount.

terms.definition: How well a finding may apply to a different population, task or operating setting. This site requires local measurement before scaling a claim.
terms.example: A student programming study may not predict an experienced team’s AppSec review effort.
